newsitem.title: INDIA: India Ambuja says to repeat 95/96 growth.
newsitem.headline: India Ambuja says to repeat 95/96 growth.

text.p: Indian cement maker Gujarat Ambuja on Tuesday announced improved financial results for the year ended June 30, 1996 and scoffed at suggestions that an emerging oversupply could slow down growth in the coming years.
The company said after-tax profits rose 47 percent to 1.48 billion rupees and stepped up dividend to 5.0 rupees per share from 4.0 rupees in the previous year.
"With increased production from its cement plants and firm cement prices, the company is expected to do well during the currrent year," it said after a board meeting on Tuesday.
A cement analyst at the Bombay office of a foreign securities firm said he did not think Gujarat Ambuja could maintain its profit growth in 1996/97.

He said a cement surplus in northern India and large capacity additions by Larsen & Toubro and others in western India, Ambuja's major markets, would lead to an oversupply which would slow down its profit growth.
But Anil Singhvi, Gujarat Ambuja's treasurer, said he didn't agree with those who forecast an oversupply in cement.
"There won't be any surplus in 1996/97," Singhvi told Reuters. "It would be an equally good year if not better."
Some analysts said the firm's profit was somewhat exaggerated because it did not provide for a minimum alternate tax (MAT) announced by the government in its July 1996 budget.
But Singhvi said MAT was yet to be approved by the parliament, which is currently debating the budget.
Gujarat Ambuja's fourth cement plant is expected to be commissioned in December 1996, taking up its total capacity to 4.5 million tonnes.
The company sold 3.1 million tonnes of cement during the year ended June 30, 1996, compared to 2.0 million tonnes during the year ago period.

The high market capitalisation, liquidity and depth of Gujarat Ambuja's share was recognised by its recent inclusion in the revamped benchmark 30-share sensitive (sensex) index of the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE).
It is the youngest among the 30 BSE sensex firms.
The year 1995/96 (April-March) was a good year for Indian cement industry. Demand grew by 12 percent and cement prices were firm throughout the year, analysts said.

"The growth momentus of 1995/96 continues during the current year also and the first quarter growth of 14 percent which is the highest ever growth achieved by the industry," the Gujarat Ambuja statement said.
"Cement demand will continue to grow at more than 8.0 percent, aided by strong GDP growth," B. Shashikanth, cement analyst at securities firm Peregrine Capital in Bombay said.

He said Gujarat Ambuja was India's lowest-cost cement producer. "This partly stems from its internal efficiencies, as well as quality limestone deposits which provides cheaper conversion costs," he said in a June cement sector report.
